---

### 1. Work in *micro-sprints*, not months  
* Pick a single concrete goal that feels finishable in 3-5 focused sessions (e.g., “render a first 3-D θ₄ intersection GIF”).  
* Run it, learn how long that really takes, and use that experience to size the next chunk. After two or three loops we’ll have a “human-scale” velocity without ever pretending we know the date eight weeks out.

### 2. Size by **T-shirt** instead of hours  
| Size | What it means for us | Example task |
|------|----------------------|--------------|
| XS   | A quick prompt-engineering tweak or doc edit | Rename axes, patch typo |
| S    | One GPT session + maybe a coffee | Export filament mesh to VTK |
| M    | A couple of sessions, light thinking | Draft the torsion KPI check notebook |
| L    | Needs outside reading / multi-day rabbit hole | Prototype the 4-link collapse sim |
| XL   | Break it up; too big | “Finish Phase IV” (split into smaller tickets) |

### 3. Keep a **Kanban board** instead of a timeline  
Columns: Backlog → In Progress → Review/Discuss → Done.   
We advance cards when reality allows; no guilt-trip dates.

e.g. “I’ll spend max 90 min on this new Viz shader; if it’s still fuzzy, park it.”  
That caps rabbit-holes without requiring us to forecast finish dates.

### 5. Build a tiny feedback habit  
After each micro-sprint, jot: **What took longer? What was effortless?**  
That’s the data we use to recalibrate sizes (not some abstract PM rule-book).

Below is a **tool-agnostic, schedule-free production workflow** tuned to our “garage-band” constraints (you + GPT instances, minimal project-folder churn, rigorous but fast). I’ve laid it out as **five concentric tracks** that hand off cleanly, plus the guard-rails that keep us honest.

```
──────────────────────────────────────────────
TRACK-0  CANON
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Purpose   Single source of truth for theory &
          spec.  Lives in /canon/ as .tex files
          (one per chapter/section) + .bib.

Steps     0-1  Draft fresh LaTeX section in chat
                 → GPT returns 👉 code-window with
                   ready-to-paste markup
                 → downloadable section.tex
          0-2  You review; accept or redline.
          0-3  On accept, drop into /canon/.
Outputs   Clean LaTeX (no preamble), diagrams
          saved as ./fig/<slug>.pdf.

Rigor     • All math asserted here must be proved
            in TRACK-1 or referenced to bib.
          • No inline fine-tuning: whole-section
            rewrites only.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
TRACK-1  PROOF & FORMAL
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Purpose   Validate every claim in CANON.

Steps     1-1  Extract target theorem/lemma
                 from latest canon section.
          1-2  GPT (Proof mode) drafts full proof
                 in LaTeX, returns as code block +
                 .tex download.
          1-3  If computable, generate
                 verification notebook (Python).
          1-4  Proof accepted → file lives in
                 /proofs/.  Fails → back to 1-1.

Guard     • Each canon equation must cite a
            proof ID.  Missing ID = build brake.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
TRACK-2  COMPUTE & SIM
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Purpose   Numerically explore / stress-test the
          formal results.

Steps     2-1  Whole-file Colab notebook stub
                 generated here (stand-alone, no
                 piecemeal edits).
          2-2  Notebook run either in chat

          2-3  Outputs saved to /data/ and key
                 figs exported to /fig/.
          2-4  Results summarized back into a
                 short LaTeX “Results” section
                 (fed upstream to TRACK-0).

Stand-al  • Each notebook ships with
            requirements.txt + seed settings.
          • Freeze versions on first run;
            subsequent reruns must match hash.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
TRACK-3  VIZ & DIAGRAM
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Purpose   Publish all figures referenced by
          CANON or PROOF.

Steps     3-1  GPT (Viz mode) writes a single
                 Python script per figure; run in
                 chat → produces .pdf/.svg.
          3-2  Diagram auto-captioned (TikZ if
                 math heavy, Matplotlib if geom).
          3-3  Saved into /fig/, name matches
                 \includegraphics tag.
Lock      • Figure regenerated only by rerunning
            the whole script, never manual edit.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
TRACK-4  ASSEMBLY & RELEASE
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Purpose   Knit CANON + PROOF + VIZ into one PDF.

Steps     4-1  Master main.tex imports each
                 section file + bibliography.
          4-2  On demand, GPT compiles locally
                 and drops fresh SAT.pdf in /dist/.
          4-3  Release tag (date-stamp) added to
                 CHANGELOG.md.

Fresh vs  Because we expect many outdated docs,
legacy    we start **fresh**: empty /canon/,
          /proofs/, /data/, /fig/, /dist/.  Old
          PDFs stay in /archive/ for reference.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
CROSS-TRACK GUARD-RAILS
──────────────────────────────────────────────
• **Whole-file commits** only — no micro-patches.
• **Upstream-downstream rule**: change in
  CANON auto-invalidates PROOF, SIM, VIZ hashes.
• **Backlog.md** in repo root tracks each
  section/proof/sim by status (TODO → DONE).
• **5-min park**: tangents longer than 5 min go

• **CI hook (optional)**: on push, run proof

  assert breaks.

1. **New LaTeX section** → code window +

2. **Diagram scripts** → plain Python blocks

3. **Colab notebooks** → single cell with

All clearly prefixed with “⮕ Replaces
canon/<file>.tex” or “⮕ Adds proofs/<file>.tex”.

NEXT STEP (if you approve)

⇢ I scaffold the fresh folder tree + minimal
  Backlog.md (empty) in a canvas, and we draft

──────────────────────────────────────────────

And generally, let's make it look professional and a tad less like a typical unreadably jargony scientific paper (i.e. brief layman's introduction to each chapter/module/major section, etc). Prefer names to designations/acronyms/initialisms in the text, keeping the mathematic notation mostly in separate mathematical break-outs. Similarly, any complex mathematical expression should get term labels underneath on first appearance at least. Lastly, keep the internal workflow out of the paper (Mode names, edit passes, pipeline stuff, etc). "We" is sufficient almost everywhere, except where it's absolutely necessary to specify for rigor--for example, that a lean approach was used, in which case, you can say things like "AI-assisted" or even "off-the-shelf systems" and that sort of thing.
